title.en: Homage to Bhava and Rudra: his names, his forms, his waters

summary: Fifteen yajus, each opening with namaḥ and naming two aspects of Rudra in the dative, each followed by ca. Sāyaṇa notes that the yajus with homage on both sides ended with the fourth anuvāka and that from the fifth to the ninth each yajus opens with homage alone. The names move from Bhava, Rudra, Śarva and Paśupati, through his appearance (blue neck and white throat, braided or shaven hair, a thousand eyes, a hundred bows), his size, age and priority, to his swiftness and his presence in the current, the wave, still water, the stream and the island. Sāyaṇa explains the two ca of each yajus as letting namaḥ go with each name separately.

vyakarana.note: From this anuvāka to the ninth every yajus opens with namaḥ and does not close with it, as those of the third and fourth did. ‘Be’ is understood.
bhava, from √bhū ‘to be, to come to be’. Dative with namaḥ (P. 2.3.16).

Each yajus of this anuvāka has two datives, each followed by ca. Sāyaṇa explains the pair at the end of the anuvāka: the ca are conjunctive and are read so that namaḥ may be construed with each dative on its own — ‘homage to A, and [homage] to B’.

translation.literal: Homage to Bhava and to Rudra.
translation.readable: Homage to Bhava, and to Rudra.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa marks the turn in the hymn: the yajus with homage on both sides ended with the fourth anuvāka («चतुर्थेऽनुवाक उभयतोनमस्काराणि यजूंषि समापितानि»), and from the fifth the yajus open with homage alone («नमस्कारोपक्रमाण्येव»). He takes Bhava as the one from whom living beings come to be («भवन्ति प्राणिनोऽस्मादिति भवः»), and Rudra as the one who drives away sorrow, the cause of weeping («रुद्रोदनहेतुभूतं दुःखं द्रावयतीति रुद्रः»).

translation.literal: Homage to Śarva and to the lord of cattle.
translation.readable: Homage to Śarva, and to Paśupati, the lord of beasts.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: Śarva is the one who crushes and destroys sin («शृणाति हिनस्ति पापमिति शर्वः»). Paśupati is the one who protects men («पुरुषान्पालयतीति पशुपतिः») who are like cattle for want of knowledge (the printed text, broken by a page number, reads «पशुसमानानज्ञा» … «निनः», that is paśusamānān ajñāninaḥ).

flags.note: The dictionaries connect śarva with śaru ‘arrow’ (‘the archer’); Sāyaṇa explains it from √śṝ, ‘he who crushes sin’. The word table gives both; the translation keeps the name.

vyakarana.note: In the bahuvrīhi the feminine nīlā (agreeing with grīvā) takes its masculine form nīla (P. 6.3.34), and the whole compound is masculine, agreeing with Rudra.
śiti ‘white’; Monier-Williams also records ‘black, dark-blue’ from later literature. Sāyaṇa takes ‘white’.

Each yajus of this anuvāka has two datives, each followed by ca. Sāyaṇa explains the pair at the end of the anuvāka: the ca are conjunctive and are read so that namaḥ may be construed with each dative on its own — ‘homage to A, and [homage] to B’.

translation.literal: Homage to the blue-necked one and to the white-throated one.
translation.readable: Homage to him whose neck is blue, and to him whose throat is white.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa reconciles the two names. Part of the neck is blue from holding the Kālakūṭa poison («कालकूटधारणेन नीलवर्णो ग्रीवैकदेशो यस्यासौ नीलग्रीवः»); the rest of the throat is white («शितिः श्वेतवर्णोऽवशिष्टः कण्ठप्रदेशो यस्यासौ शितिकण्ठः»).
units.reflection: Two colours are named on one throat, side by side. Sāyaṇa does not choose between them; he places both.

vyakarana.note: kaparda ‘braid, knot of hair’ with the possessive suffix -in (P. 5.2.115); dative kapardine. A derivative, not a compound.
vyupta is vi + upta, the past passive participle of √vap ‘to shear’ with samprasāraṇa (P. 6.1.15); vi + u gives vyu inside the word.

translation.literal: Homage to the one with braided hair and to the one with shorn hair.
translation.readable: Homage to him who wears his hair in braids, and to him whose head is shaven.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: kapardin is the one who has kaparda, the mass of matted locks («कपर्दो जटाजूटो यस्यास्तीति कपर्दी»); vyuptakeśa is the shaven-headed one («मुण्डितकेशो»; the name itself is misprinted व्युप्ककेशः). He resolves the contrast by guise: the matted locks in the dress of the Pāśupatas and others («पाशुपतादिवेषेण कपर्दित्वम्»), the shaven head in the dress of ascetics («यत्यादिवेषेण मुण्डितकेशत्वम्»).

translation.literal: Homage to the thousand-eyed one and to the one with a hundred bows.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: the thousand eyes belong to him in the guise of Indra («इन्द्रवेषेण»); the hundred bows to him as the descent with a thousand arms («सहस्रभुजावतारित्वेन»), furnished with bows numbering a hundred («शतसंख्याकैः»).

samasa.meaning: one who lies on the mountain
one who has entered into (is pervaded by) the śipis — in Monier-Williams ‘pervaded by rays’

vyakarana.note: giri ‘mountain’ + -śa from √śī ‘to lie, rest’, as Sāyaṇa analyses it (शेते).
viṣṭa is the past passive participle of √viś ‘to enter’. The first member śipi is obscure: Monier-Williams gives ‘a ray of light’ (from the Nirukta) and ‘= paśu’ (from the Taittirīya Saṃhitā).

translation.literal: Homage to the one who lies on the mountain and to Śipiviṣṭa.
translation.readable: Homage to him who dwells on the mountain, and to Śipiviṣṭa.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: giriśa is the one who lies, that is abides, on the mountain Kailāsa («गिरौ कैलासे शेते तिष्ठतीति गिरिशः»). Śipiviṣṭa is the one who bears the form of Viṣṇu («विष्णुमूर्तिधारी शिपिविष्टः»), on the authority of the śruti «विष्णुः शिपिविष्टः» that he quotes.

flags.note: Sāyaṇa does not analyse śipiviṣṭa here; he identifies the bearer of the name. The samāsa entry follows Monier-Williams (‘pervaded by rays’), and the sense of śipi is not secure; the translation keeps the name.

vyakarana.note: mīḍhvas is the Vedic perfect participle of √mih ‘to shed, to pour (water)’, formed without reduplication (P. 6.1.12); its weak stem mīḍhuṣ- takes the superlative -tama, and ṣ + t gives ṣṭ (P. 8.4.41). A derivative, not a compound.

translation.literal: Homage to the most bountiful one and to the one who has arrows.
translation.readable: Homage to the most bountiful, and to him who bears arrows.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: mīḍhuṣṭama is the one who, in the form of the cloud, sends abundant rain («मेघरूपेणात्यन्तं वर्षयिता»; the name is misprinted भीढुष्टमः); iṣumat is the bearer of arrows («बाणधारक इषुमान्»).

translation.literal: Homage to the short one and to the dwarf.
translation.readable: Homage to him who is short, and to him who is a dwarf.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa distinguishes the two: shortness is smallness of the body’s measure («शरीरेऽल्पप्रमाणत्वं ह्रस्वत्वम्»); dwarfishness comes from the contraction of limbs such as the fingers («संकोचाद्वामनत्वम्»).

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: bṛhat is the one large in shape («आकारेण प्रौढो बृहन्»); varṣīyas the one abundant in good qualities («गुणैः»; the printed text reads सगृद्धो, evidently for samṛddhaḥ ‘abundant’).
units.reflection: Short and dwarfish in one yajus, great and greater in the next: the hymn does not hold him to one size.

sam + vṛdhvan, a stem in -van from √vṛdh; dative -vane. The text writes सव्ँवृध्वने: the m of sam before v is written as the nasalised v̐ of the Taittirīya text. The padaccheda uses the ordinary anusvāra.

translation.literal: Homage to the grown one and to the one who grows fully.
translation.readable: Homage to him who is aged, and to him who grows to fullness.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: vṛddha is the one greater in age («वयसाऽधिको वृद्धः»); saṃvṛdhvan the one made to grow fully by praises (printed «सन्यक्स्तृतिभिर्वर्धितः संवृध्वा», evidently for samyak stutibhir vardhitaḥ).

flags.note: saṃvṛdhvan has no entry in Monier-Williams. The analysis sam + √vṛdh + -van is the editor’s; Sāyaṇa gives the sense (vardhitaḥ, ‘made to grow’) but not the formation.

units.reflection: In Sāyaṇa’s reading the pair is the moving wave and the silent pool; both are places where Rudra is named.

words.context: Sāyaṇa: present on the island, land in the midst of water
the second ca of the pair; the anuvāka ends here

sandhi.rule: visarga before a sibilant may become that sibilant (P. 8.3.36); the Taittirīya text writes the doubled sibilant

vyakarana.note: srotas ‘stream, current’ with -ya, ‘being in’.
dvīpa ‘island’ with -ya, ‘being on’; Monier-Williams ‘living on an island’.

Each yajus of this anuvāka has two datives, each followed by ca. Sāyaṇa explains the pair at the end of the anuvāka: the ca are conjunctive and are read so that namaḥ may be construed with each dative on its own — ‘homage to A, and [homage] to B’.

translation.literal: Homage to the one in the stream and to the one on the island.
translation.readable: Homage to him who is in the stream, and to him who is on the island.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: srotasya is the one present in the current («प्रवाहे स्थितः»); dvīpya the one present on the island, the land in the midst of the water («द्वीपे वारिमध्यवर्तिभूमौ स्थितो»). He closes the anuvāka with the rule for every yajus in it: the two ca are read as conjunctive so that namaḥ is construed with each of the two datives separately («अत्रैकैकस्मिन्यजुषि चतुर्थ्यन्ताभ्यां पदाभ्यां नमःशब्दं पृथगन्वेतुं समुच्चयार्थौ चकारौ पठितौ»).
